summary: Describes the Handle System namespace and service in detail. The namespace definition specifies handle syntax and semantic structure, and the data model defines data structures the protocol uses. It also covers service and operation models. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If the Handle System is a giant address book, this is its rule book. It says how names are spelled, what information is kept, and how the book is run.

questions: handle system namespace and service definition
subtitle: The rules for naming, data structures, and how the Handle System works.

tldr.problem: The Handle System needs detailed specifications for how handles are named, what information can be stored with them, how that information is structured, and how services cooperate to manage and deliver handle data.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3651 defines the handle namespace syntax, a data model with pre-defined value types for administration and service information, a hierarchical service architecture with a Global Handle Registry and Local Handle Services, and an operation model for how clients find services and complete transactions.
tldr.outcome: Implementers can build compatible handle servers and clients that interoperate to create a global distributed name service where handles remain consistent across all implementations.

facts.label: Naming authority levels
facts.value: Hierarchical tree structure with dot-separated segments

facts.label: Pre-defined value types
facts.value: 7 types: HS_ADMIN, HS_SITE, HS_NA_DELEGATE, HS_SERV, HS_ALIAS, HS_PRIMARY, HS_VLIST

facts.label: Service hierarchy levels
facts.value: Global Handle Registry (1) + Local Handle Services (unlimited)

facts.label: Handle value fields
facts.value: Index, type, data, permissions, TTL, timestamp, references

today: RFC 3651 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It remains the authoritative specification for the Handle System namespace and service architecture.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 3651 provides the detailed technical foundation for the Handle System, specifying the namespace definition, data model, service model, and operation model. This document is intended for implementers building handle servers and clients, as well as administrators managing naming authorities. It assumes readers understand the overview from RFC 3650 and provides the precise rules for how all Handle System components must work together.

The specification covers four main areas: how handles are syntactically constructed and what characters they can contain; what data structures can be stored with each handle and their meaning; how the service architecture is organized with central and local components; and the detailed procedure for clients to find the right server and complete transactions.
sections.eli5: This is the detailed rule book for how the Handle System works. It tells implementers exactly what is allowed and how everything must be organized.

sections.title: Handle Namespace and Syntax
sections.content:
Handles are UTF-8 encoded Unicode strings consisting of two parts: the naming authority and the local name, separated by a forward slash. The naming authority identifies the organization or administrative unit (such as 10.1045 for D-Lib Magazine), and the local name uniquely identifies the resource within that authority. Naming authorities are hierarchical, using dots to separate levels like a tree: the root level might be 10, with children like 10.1045, 10.2000, and so on. This structure prevents collisions while allowing any organization to join the global namespace by obtaining a unique naming authority prefix.

The RFC specifies exactly which Unicode characters are allowed in handles and encoding requirements. Handles must be encoded as UTF-8 for transmission over networks. By default, handle servers treat handles as case-sensitive, though a server can choose to be case-insensitive for ASCII characters. This flexibility allows existing local naming systems to integrate with the global Handle System.
sections.eli5: A handle looks like prefix/name where the prefix is unique to an organization and the name is unique within that organization. Together they form a globally unique identifier.

sections.title: Data Structures and Value Types
sections.content:
Each handle can have multiple values assigned to it. Every value is a record containing an index, a type, the data itself, access permissions, a time-to-live (TTL), a timestamp, and optional references to other values. Each value is uniquely identified within its handle by an index number. The type field identifies the kind of data, such as URL, EMAIL, or other application-specific types. The permission field controls who can read or write the value, using bit-flags like PUBLIC_READ (anyone can see it), ADMIN_READ (only administrators can see it), PUBLIC_WRITE (anyone can modify it), and so on. The TTL specifies how long a cached copy of the value is valid.

RFC 3651 defines seven pre-defined value types that are essential to the Handle System's operation. HS_ADMIN defines administrators and their permissions for a handle. HS_SITE contains the network address, port, and public key of a handle server. HS_SERV is an indirection mechanism for shared service information. HS_ALIAS supports renaming by pointing one handle to another. HS_NA_DELEGATE designates which handle service manages child naming authorities. HS_PRIMARY specifies which service sites are primary for a distributed service. HS_VLIST creates lists of handle value references, useful for grouping administrators. These types are reserved and have special meaning to the protocol.
sections.eli5: Each handle value is like a database record: it has a type (what kind of information it is), the actual data, and rules about who can read or change it and for how long it's valid.

sections.title: Service Components and Hierarchical Architecture
sections.content:
The Handle System service is organized hierarchically with a single Global Handle Registry (GHR) at the top and unlimited Local Handle Services (LHS) below it. The GHR manages the naming authorities themselves (stored as handles under the reserved naming authority 0.NA) and directs clients to the responsible LHS for any naming authority. Each LHS manages handles under one or more naming authorities assigned to it. Every service, whether the GHR or any LHS, is distributed: it can have multiple geographic service sites, and each site can have multiple server computers. This distribution avoids single points of failure and allows load balancing. The GHR service information is stored in the root handle 0.NA/0.NA, which clients can query to find current GHR locations and public keys for verifying signatures.

Clients initially need only the GHR service information to bootstrap. To resolve any handle, a client queries the GHR for the naming authority's entry, receives the address and public key of the LHS managing that naming authority, and then queries that LHS. Clients can cache service information based on its TTL to avoid repeated queries. The RFC also defines optional middleware components like caching servers and proxy servers that reduce latency and provide alternative access methods (such as HTTP) for clients.
sections.eli5: One central server (the GHR) knows which organization manages each handle prefix. Other servers (the LHS) manage the actual handles. Clients ask the central server where to go, then ask the right organization's server for the answer.

sections.title: How Clients and Servers Interact
sections.content:
The operation model describes two types of service operations: resolution and administration. Resolution means querying for handle values; administration means adding, deleting, or modifying handles and values. Both are request-response interactions. A client sends a request to a server, which responds with either an answer, a referral to another service component, a challenge requesting authentication, or an error. For administration and sensitive queries, the server can authenticate the client using a challenge-response protocol that supports both secret-key and public-key cryptography. A client proves its identity by demonstrating knowledge of a secret key or possession of a private key. Sessions can be established to share authentication information and TCP connections across multiple operations, and can be encrypted using a session key for data confidentiality.

RFC 3651 also specifies that clients can verify server responses using digital signatures. Each server has a public key available through the service information in the HS_SITE record. Clients can request that servers sign their responses, then verify the signature using the public key. This protects against man-in-the-middle attacks and allows clients to trust responses even over untrusted networks.
sections.eli5: Clients ask servers for information or to make changes. Servers can check that clients are really who they claim to be, and clients can verify that responses really came from the legitimate server.
